title: Chapter 75: Distance 2
content:
Chapter 75

Distance 2

The trio tore across the sky, barreling toward the Burial Mounds like a shot from a bow. The moment the blackened, brooding peak pierced through the clouds, Wei Wuxian’s stomach dropped.

Even from a distance, guttural shrieks and snarls echoed up from the dark woods—not from just one or two rogue corpses, but a whole frenzied horde. Lan Wangji pinched a hand seal, and Bichen surged forward with a sudden burst of speed, yet remained as smooth and level as glass.

The instant their boots touched the dirt, a shadow bolted from the tree line, screeching as it lunged for an older man on the ground. A flash of azure light flickered, and Bichen cleaved the monster clean in two. Pinned to the mud, the man turned paper-white. Seeing Wei Wuxian step into view, he cried out, "Young Master Wei!"

Wei Wuxian flicked a paper charm from his wrist, barking, "Fourth Uncle, what the hell happened?!"

Fourth Uncle choked out, "The Demon-Subduing Cave... the corpses sealed inside, they've all broken out!"

"I set wards across the threshold!" Wei Wuxian countered. "Who tampered with them?!"

"No one touched a thing! It was... it was..."

Before he could finish, a sharp, furious shout cut through the trees. "A-Ning!"

Further in the gloom, a dozen Wen cultivators had formed a defensive ring around a terrifying figure. It was Wen Ning, his eyes rolled back to a milky, pupilless white, his features twisted into an unhinged snarl. The sea of containment charms once plastered across his skin was shredded to scraps. In his iron grip he dragged two fierce corpses, practically torn to ribbons with his bare hands—dripping black blood, their flesh reduced to mangled pulp over splintered bone. Yet he kept thrashing them against the rocks, as if he wouldn't be satisfied until he had ground their very marrow into dust.

Standing at the front of the defensive line, blade raised, was Wen Qing.

Wei Wuxian roared, "Didn't I tell you not to touch the talismans on him?!"

Wen Qing didn't even have the luxury to be shocked by Lan Wangji's sudden appearance. "Nobody touched them! Nobody even set foot near the cave! He went berserk and ripped them off himself! He didn't just shred his own bindings—he tore down the perimeter wards and smashed the Blood Pool! The corpses soaking inside have all crawled out! Wei Wuxian, get over to Granny and the others, they can't hold out much longer!!!"

A sickening hiss slithered from the canopy overhead. Looking up, several corpses had actually scaled the massive ancient pines, coiled like snakes across the high branches, baring jagged fangs that dripped vile, putrid slime. Wen Ning’s head snapped up. Catching sight of them, he dropped the mangled carcasses in his hands, coiled his legs, and launched himself skyward—straight into the treetops!

The tree stood at least fifty feet tall, yet he cleared the distance in a single, terrifying leap. The explosive force was monstrous. The moment his boots hit the branches, Wen Ning swung his arms, tearing the perched corpses apart in a flurry of severed limbs, showering the soil below in a foul rain of black blood. Unsatisfied, he threw himself toward the next ridge.

Wei Wuxian drew Chenqing. "Lan—!"

He had meant to ask Lan Wangji to prioritize the defenseless elderly while he handled Wen Ning. But glancing over his shoulder, the white-robed cultivator had already vanished into thin air. Right as panic flared, a resonant, booming chord of guqin notes tore through the trees like thunder, scattering a flurry of frantic crows into the sky. Without needing to be told, Lan Wangji was already on it.

Wei Wuxian breathed an inward sigh of relief, bringing the dark bamboo to his lips. Chenqing let loose a sharp, piercing wail.

Touching down on the rocks, Wen Ning’s brutal momentum hitched. Seizing the opening, Wei Wuxian called out, "Wen Ning! Do you recognize me?!"

Across the ridge, the zither resonated three times before cutting into sudden silence—meaning Lan Wangji had subdued the rogue corpses within three beats of his strings. Wen Ning crouched low, a feral, rattling hiss scraping from his throat, tensing like a coiled, cornered beast ready to snap.

Wei Wuxian lifted the flute to play again, only to feel a sudden weight tugging at his knee. Looking down, Wen Yuan was still clamped around his calf, trembling in petrified silence. He had completely forgotten he was holding a toddler!

Yanking the boy up by his collar, Wei Wuxian tossed him toward Wen Qing. "Take him and run!"

Right in that split second of distraction, Wen Ning pounced.

It hit like a falling boulder. The concussive impact launched Wei Wuxian backward through the air, his spine slamming violently into the trunk of a massive cedar. Searing heat surged up his throat, and a raw curse spilled from his lips.

Lan Wangji reappeared just in time to see the blow land, his pristine composure shattering into pure horror as he threw himself forward. Wen Qing had barely shoved the kid into another cultivator's arms to check on Wei Wuxian, only to find herself beaten to the punch.

Lan Wangji practically gathered Wei Wuxian against his chest, catching his hand in a tight, unyielding grip as he immediately began pouring spiritual energy into his meridians.

Wen Qing blurted out, "Let go of him, you don't need to do that! Let me see him! I'm Wen Qing!"

As the most renowned physician of the Qishan Wen Clan, her skill was unmatched. Only then did Lan Wangji stop the infusion, shifting aside to let her examine the injury—though his fingers never loosened their iron grip around Wei Wuxian’s hand.

Wei Wuxian shoved him away with a grimace. "Don't let him get past!"

Having struck him down, Wen Ning's arms hung limp at his sides as he lumbered toward the lower slope—the exact direction where the rest of the Wen survivors had barricaded themselves.

Wen Qing screamed down the valley, "Run! Get out of there! He's heading straight for you!"

Wei Wuxian tore himself from Lan Wangji's grasp, swallowing down the copper tang in his throat as he bolted after him. Lan Wangji matched him stride for stride. "Where is your sword?!"

Wei Wuxian flicked twelve yellow talismans from his sleeve, barking, "Lost it ages ago!"

The twelve charms aligned in mid-air, bursting into a synchronized blaze that slammed onto Wen Ning’s back like a leash of fire, pulling him up short. Lan Wangji flicked the strings of his guqin behind his back; a ripple of spiritual wire snagged Wen Ning’s boots, forcing the creature to a grinding, shuddering halt.

Wei Wuxian pressed Chenqing to his lips. Having just taken a concussive hit to the chest, a spray of bloody froth sputtered over the mouthpiece. His brow pinched tight, but he gritted his teeth against the agonizing churn in his ribs, forcing a smooth, flawless melody through the dark.

Trapped beneath the combined onslaught of flute and zither, Wen Ning dropped hard to his knees, throwing his head back in a ragged, deafening howl that rattled the canopy overhead. Wei Wuxian finally lost his grip, coughing up a mouthful of dark crimson.

Wangji’s strings snapped into an ear-splitting screech. Wen Ning clutched his skull, shrieking in pure agony as he curled into a tight ball on the dirt.

Wen Qing cried out, her voice shredded with tears: "A-Ning! A-Ning!" She lunged forward, but Wei Wuxian caught her shoulder. "Stay back!"

Seeing her brother writhing in torment beneath the relentless musical assault broke her heart. She knew that holding back against a berserk fierce corpse was suicide, yet she couldn't bear to watch him suffer. Turning to the white-robed prodigy, she pleaded, "Hanguang-jun, show some mercy!"

Wei Wuxian called out, "Lan Zhan! Take it easy on—"

"...M... Master..."

Wei Wuxian froze mid-breath. "Wait..."

He shouted, "Lan Zhan, stop the chords!"

That voice had come straight from Wen Ning.

Lan Wangji brought his palm flat against the strings, silencing the vibrating reverberations instantly.

Wei Wuxian stepped closer, stunned. "Wen Ning?!"

Wen Ning lifted his head with agonizing, jerky movements.

Staring back from his sunken eye sockets was no longer a pair of terrifying, milky-white voids, but... two distinct, dark irises.

Wen Ning parted his lips, struggling to push out the syllables: "...Young... Master... Wei...?"

Every word sounded like pulling teeth, as if his tongue were too swollen to navigate his jaws. But it was distinctly, unmistakably human speech—not a mindless, guttural roar.

Wen Qing stood completely paralyzed.

After an endless, suffocating beat, a strangled scream tore from her lungs. She threw herself across the dirt, bawling, "A-Ning!"

The impact sent both of them tumbling into the mud. Wen Ning rasped, "Jie... Jie..."

Wen Qing wrapped her arms around her brother's cold shoulders, sobbing and laughing hysterically as she buried her face against his chest. "It's me! It's your sister, it's Jie! A-Ning!"

She cried his name over and over like a litany. The surrounding Wen cultivators looked as though they wanted to swarm in for a group embrace, but didn't dare intrude; instead, they threw their arms around one another, weeping and laughing in chaotic relief. Fourth Uncle sprinted down the slope at top speed, yelling into the night: "He's back! It worked! It actually worked! A-Ning is awake...!"

Wei Wuxian walked over, crouching beside Wen Ning. "How are you feeling?"

Wen Ning lay flat on his back, his limbs and neck still moving with stiff, wooden resistance. "I... I..." He choked on his words for a long moment before finally mumbling, "...I really want to cry, but no tears are coming out. Why is that...?"

Wei Wuxian let out a quiet, tender chuckle, patting his shoulder. "You remember, right? You're dead, buddy."

Confirming that Wen Ning’s consciousness had truly returned, Wei Wuxian exhaled a breath he felt like he’d been holding for months.

He had actually pulled it off.

Back then, swept up in blind, murderous fury, he had hastily raised Wen Ning as a low-level fierce corpse. Though it gave Wen Ning the chance to identify and tear apart the overseers who had tortured him to death, seeing him reduced to a mindless, snarling beast—drooling for raw meat and snapping like a rabid dog—had broken Wen Qing's spirit completely.

Once his head cooled, Wei Wuxian had made her a bold promise: he would find a way to restore her brother's mind. But the truth was, it had been pure bravado, spun solely to keep her from unraveling. He had zero roadmap, walking a tightrope in pitch darkness.

Days and nights of tearing his hair out, skipping meals and sleep... and against all odds, he had delivered on his word.

Wen Qing cradled Wen Ning’s pale face, fat tears rolling down her cheeks, finally breaking into raw, breathless wails—just as she had the night she first held his cold body. Wen Ning’s stiff, clumsy fingers gently patted her back. More and more Wen remnants climbed up from the foot of the hill; some threw themselves into the sobbing heap, while others looked toward Wei Wuxian and Lan Wangji with eyes overflowing with trembling awe and gratitude.

Knowing the siblings needed their privacy—and that a woman as fiercely proud as Wen Qing would hate having outsiders witness her messy tears—Wei Wuxian turned around. "Lan Zhan."

Lan Wangji looked at him.

Wei Wuxian tilted his chin toward the trail. "Since you're already here, want to come in and take a seat?"

They walked up to a yawning, jagged cave mouth venting drafts of bone-chilling air.

Lan Wangji paused. "The Demon-Subduing Cave?"

Wei Wuxian beamed. "Yep. Named it myself. Catchy, right?"

Lan Wangji stayed characteristically quiet.

Wei Wuxian teased, "Come on, I know what you're thinking: 'It's terrible.' Word traveled, and I've heard the chatter—people gossiping about how a demonic rogue like me, an arch-villain through and through, has the audacity to call his den the 'Demon-Subduing Cave.'"

Lan Wangji offered neither agreement nor denial. They crossed the threshold, Wei Wuxian’s easy laughter bouncing off the hollow stone walls. "They've got it all backward, honestly. It doesn't mean what they think it means."

"How so?"

"Simple," Wei Wuxian shrugged. "I sleep here all the time. A cave where a demon slumbers flat on the ground—isn't that literally a Demon-Subduing Cave?"

Lan Wangji stayed silent.

Entering the primary cavern, Lan Wangji asked, "And the Blood Pool?"

Wei Wuxian pointed toward an ominous basin of dark liquid tucked into the rock. "Right there."

The chamber was bathed in gloomy shadows; the water looked somewhere between pitch-black and bruised crimson, exhaling a faint, sickly metallic tang. The protective boundary array originally strung around the rim had been snapped by Wen Ning’s rampage; Wei Wuxian casually gathered the severed cords, tying them back together and reinforcing the knots with a flick of spiritual energy.

Lan Wangji observed, "The yin energy runs exceptionally deep."

"It does," Wei Wuxian agreed. "Heavy malice makes it the perfect nursery for dark things. I use it to marinate a few half-finished fierce corpses. Care to guess how many are resting at the bottom?" He flashed a sharp grin. "Truth is, I lost count myself. The water's been smelling more and more like fresh blood lately, though."

Perhaps it was a trick of the dim cavern light, but Wei Wuxian’s complexion looked ghost-pale, and that casual smirk carried an unnerving, shadowy chill.

Lan Wangji looked at him intently. "Wei Ying."

"Yeah?"

"Can you truly keep this under control?"

Wei Wuxian blinked. "Keep what under control? Wen Ning? Absolutely. Look at him, his mind is back. The first of his kind in history." A flash of boyish pride lit his face.

"What if he loses control again?"

"I've got the hang of reining him in now," Wei Wuxian waved it off. "He's tethered to me; as long as I don't lose it, he won't either."

Silence hung in the air.

Lan Wangji asked quietly, "And what if you lose control?"

Wei Wuxian’s tone flattened. "I won't."

"How can you be sure?"

"I won't," Wei Wuxian said, his voice hard as iron. "And I can't afford to."

Lan Wangji looked around the bleak cavern. "Do you truly intend to live like this forever?"

"What's wrong with living like this? Looking down on my estate? This mountain peak is bigger than your Cloud Recesses, and our meals have way more flavor."

"Wei Ying," Lan Wangji cut in, his voice low and solemn. "You know that is not what I meant."

Wei Wuxian sighed, rubbing his neck. "Lan Zhan, you really are something else. I deliberately changed the subject, and you dragged it right back."

A sudden tickle caught in his throat. His chest heaved with a violent churn of stale blood, and Wei Wuxian muffled a pair of ragged coughs into his fist. Seeing Lan Wangji step forward to reach for his wrist, Wei Wuxian dodged aside. "What are you doing?"

"Your injuries."

"Forget it," Wei Wuxian brushed him off. "Why waste spiritual energy on a scratch? I'll just sit down for a bit and walk it off."

Refusing to indulge his stubbornness, Lan Wangji reached for him again. Just then, footsteps brushed the gravel outside. Wen Qing’s crisp voice echoed into the cave: "'Walk it off'? Do I look dead to you?"

Trailing behind her was Wen Ning, balancing a wooden tea tray. His skin remained a waxy, corpse-pale white, the dark ink of containment runes still faintly visible along his collar. Clamped around Wen Ning’s shin was Wen Yuan. The toddler spotted Wei Wuxian, scurried over, and smoothly transferred his little grip to Wei Wuxian’s leg instead.

Catching their eyes on him, Wen Ning’s lips twitched as if trying to smile, but his dead facial muscles refused to cooperate. He settled for an awkward bow. "Young Master Wei... Young Master Lan."

Wei Wuxian lifted his leg, swinging the dangling child back and forth like a pendulum. "What brought you two in here? Done crying already?"

"Just wait until I make you cry," Wen Qing snapped, though her voice still carried a thick, nasal stuffiness.

Wei Wuxian laughed. "As if you could make me—aghh!"

Wen Qing stepped up and delivered a concussive smack straight between his shoulder blades. The strike knocked a mouthful of congealed, black blood right out of Wei Wuxian’s chest.

He stared at her in mock betrayal, wheezing, "You... you vicious woman..." His eyes rolled back, and he dramatically went limp.

Lan Wangji’s face drained of color as he caught him. "Wei Ying!"

Wen Qing casually flicked three gleaming silver acupuncture needles between her fingers, barking, "I have plenty more where that came from. Get up!"

Wei Wuxian popped right back up from Lan Wangji’s arms as if nothing had happened, wiping the dark blood from his mouth with the back of his hand. "Never mind! A woman's wrath is lethal; I'll pass on the demonstration."

That smack had merely cleared the stagnant, bruised blood pooling in his lungs. How could the premier physician of Qishan ever misjudge her own strength? Realizing he’d been duped by another childish prank, Lan Wangji snapped his sleeves back, deliberately turning his back to them, entirely done indulging such nonsense.

Wen Ning, whose resurrected cognitive functions were still running on a slight delay, stood bewildered. Remembering that he was the one who had bruised Wei Wuxian in the first place, guilt crept onto his face. "Master, I'm... I'm so sorry..."

Wei Wuxian waved a hand dismissively. "Enough of that. You really think a love-tap from you could take me down?"

Wen Qing’s dark eyes flicked over to Lan Wangji’s stiff, turned back. "Hanguang-jun, won't you take a seat?"

A lightbulb went off in Wei Wuxian’s head; he’d felt like he was forgetting something, realizing Lan Wangji had been standing like a pillar this entire time. The only furniture in the cave consisted of a few flat stone slabs acting as beds, every single one smothered in an appalling mess—flags, daggers, wooden boxes, blood-stained bandages, half-eaten fruit cores. An absolute disaster zone.

Wei Wuxian winced. "There's nowhere to sit, really..."

Wen Qing countered coldly, "Of course there is."

With a sweeping, ruthless flick of her arm, she wiped every scrap of junk off the nearest stone bed, sending it clattering across the floor. "Look. Plenty of room."

Wei Wuxian gaped. "Hey!"

Wen Ning chimed in gently, "Yes, Young Master Lan... please sit, have some tea..." He held the tray out toward him. Resting atop the wood were two porcelain cups, scrubbed immaculately clean.

Wei Wuxian peeked inside. "Look at this poverty—serving a guest plain tap water, not a single tea leaf in sight!"

Wen Ning mumbled, "I checked the pantry... Fourth Uncle said we ran out of tea leaves..."

Wei Wuxian took a cup, sipping the water. "Unacceptable. Next time we have guests, we need to stock up." The words left his mouth before the absurdity hit him. What 'next time'? What 'guests'?

Wen Qing scoffed, "You have the nerve to complain? Every time I send you down the mountain for provisions, you come back with useless junk. Where are the radish seeds I asked for today?"

Wei Wuxian protested, "What junk?! I bought fun toys for A-Yuan! Right, A-Yuan?"

Wen Yuan ratted him out without skipping a beat: "Xian-gege is lying. The other brother bought them for me."

Wei Wuxian gasped in outrage. "You little traitor!"

Laughter rippled through the cavern. Then, without uttering a single word, Lan Wangji turned and walked toward the exit.

Wen Qing and Wen Ning froze. Wei Wuxian called after him, "Lan Zhan?"

Lan Wangji’s stride hitched for a fraction of a second. His voice was completely unreadable: "It is time I returned."

He stepped past the threshold without looking back. Wen Ning’s face fell, terrified he had somehow caused offense.

Wen Yuan panicked, calling out, "Brother!"

The toddler tried to scramble after him on his stubby legs, but Wei Wuxian scooped him up, tucking him securely under his arm. "Wait here for me."

Taking long strides, Wei Wuxian caught up to the white silhouette along the path. "Leaving already? I'll walk you down."

Lan Wangji walked in silence.

Dangling beneath Wei Wuxian’s arm, Wen Yuan tilted his chin up, asking innocently, "Isn't the brother staying for dinner?"

Lan Wangji glanced down, his pale hand reaching out to gently pat the boy’s messy hair.

Assuming the gesture meant he was staying, Wen Yuan beamed, whispering, "A-Yuan overheard a big secret... they said we're having lots of yummy food today..."

Wei Wuxian sighed, "This brother has food waiting for him at home. He can't stay."

Wen Yuan gave a soft, disappointed "Oh," his head drooping as he clamped his mouth shut.

The two men walked in silence, a toddler swaying between them, trailing the desolate path down to the foot of the Burial Mounds. Both stopped at the perimeter barrier in unison. Neither spoke.

After a long quiet, Wei Wuxian broke the silence: "Lan Zhan. Earlier, you asked if I planned on living like this forever. Truth is, I want to ask someone that too. If I don't live like this... what else am I supposed to do?"

He looked out over the barren rocks. "Abandon the demonic path? What happens to the people on this mountain then?

"Abandon them to their deaths? I can't do that. And I know damn well that if you were in my shoes, you couldn't either."

He turned, his eyes searching Lan Wangji's face. "Is there anyone out there who can show me a wide, sunlit avenue? A path where I don't have to touch demonic cultivation, but can still protect the people I need to protect?"

Lan Wangji met his gaze, offering no answer. But both of them knew the truth in their bones.

There was no such road.

It was an impossible riddle.

Wei Wuxian’s voice dropped, soft and steady. "Thank you for keeping me company today. And thank you for telling me about my Shijie’s wedding. But right and wrong lie within oneself, praise and blame belong to others, and gains and losses are not worth counting. I know what I have to do. And I believe in my own control."

As if he had anticipated that answer from the very beginning, Lan Wangji looked away, his long lashes fluttering shut.

And with that, they parted ways.

Trekking back up the mountain trail, it finally dawned on Wei Wuxian that he had promised to treat Lan Wangji to a meal—only for them to part on decidedly somber terms. And, naturally, he had completely forgotten to settle the bill.

Ah, well, Wei Wuxian thought, rubbing his nose. Lan Zhan is loaded anyway; footing the bill one more time won't break his bank. Surely he had extra silver on him—buying a few wooden toys couldn't have cleaned him out. Worst-case scenario, I'll just treat him next time... As if there's ever going to be a next time.

Looking back on it, almost every encounter they shared seemed destined to end in bitter, uncomfortable estrangement. Perhaps they truly weren't cut out to be friends.

Then again, there wouldn't be many chances left to try anyway.

Wen Yuan held his hand with one fist and clutched his little wooden sword in the other, the woven grass butterfly balanced precariously on his head. "Xian-gege, will Rich-gege come visit again?"

Wei Wuxian nearly spat out his drink. "Who on earth is 'Rich-gege'?"

Wen Yuan answered with total toddler earnestness: "The brother who has money. That makes him Rich-gege."

"Then what does that make me?"

Sure enough, Wen Yuan didn't miss a beat. "You're Xian-gege. Broke-gege."

Wei Wuxian gave him a dry side-eye, suddenly swiping the grass butterfly right off his head. "Oh, so just because he's loaded, you like him better?"

Wen Yuan stood on his tiptoes, scrambling frantically for it. "Give it back! He bought that for me!"

Wei Wuxian, being the delightfully petty manchild that he was, found endless joy in messing with toddlers. He perched the butterfly on his own head instead. "Not a chance. You were literally calling him 'Daddy' back there! What do you call me? Just 'gege'! I'm getting demoted an entire generation down the ladder for nothing!"

Wen Yuan hopped up and down, protesting, "I didn't call him Daddy!"

"I heard you loud and clear. Nope, not having it. I want a title that outranks both 'gege' and 'Daddy.' What are you gonna call me?"

Wen Yuan looked thoroughly aggrieved, his little lip trembling. "B-but... A-Yuan doesn't wanna call you Mommy... That's so weird..."

Wei Wuxian choked on air a second time. "Who said anything about Mommy?! What outranks a brother and a dad is a granddad, don't you know anything? If you're really that crazy about him, you should've spoken up earlier—I would've let him pack you off right then and there. Sure, his family's filthy rich, but their house is absolute nightmare fuel. He'd lock you in a room and make you copy ancient rulebooks from dawn till dusk. Terrified yet?"

Wen Yuan shook his head violently, whispering timidly, "...I'm not going... I still want Granny."

Wei Wuxian leaned down, zeroing in like an interrogator. "You want Granny, but you don't want me?"

Wen Yuan quickly tried to butter him up. "I do! I want Xian-gege too!" He began counting on his chubby fingers, listing them off one by one: "And Rich-gege, and Qing-jiejie, Ning-gege, Fourth Uncle, Sixth Uncle..."

Wei Wuxian tossed the butterfly back onto the boy's head. "Alright, alright, that's enough. I'm practically drowned in that crowd of yours."

Wen Yuan quickly shoved the grass butterfly deep into his pocket, terrified it might get snatched again, and pressed on, "So is Rich-gege coming back or not?"

Wei Wuxian kept a faint smile on his face.

After a long pause, he murmured softly, "Probably not."

"Why?" Wen Yuan's face fell, thoroughly dejected.

"No reason," Wei Wuxian said lightly. "Everyone in this world has their own business to take care of, their own roads to walk. People have enough on their plates keeping their own houses in order—who has the time to constantly orbit around someone else?"

They were never meant to walk the same path, after all.

Wen Yuan gave a small, half-comprehending "Oh," his little shoulders slumping in disappointment.

Wei Wuxian scooped him up in one fluid motion, tucking the boy under his arm like a sack of groceries, humming a jaunty little tune: "Let the bustling crowds take the grand, sunlit avenue; I'll stick to my single-log bridge until it goes pitch black... Walk! It! Until it goes... wait, black?"

The second the word left his mouth, he blinked. It wasn't black at all.

Usually, the summit was shrouded in suffocating, pitch-black gloom by the time he hiked back up. Tonight, however, the place looked completely transformed.

The dirt around the ramshackle shacks had been swept spotless, and even the overgrown weeds had been thoroughly cleared away. Hanging from the branches of the nearby trees were several round, crimson lanterns. They were clearly crude, homemade affairs woven from scrap wood and paper, but they glowed with a warm, steady amber light, casting a cozy golden haze across the pitch-black mountain woods.

Usually by this hour, the fifty-odd Wen remnants would have already choked down their sparse rations, blown out their oil lamps, and curled up inside their broken shacks for the night. Yet tonight, every single one of them was crowded beneath the largest open-air shelter. Supported by eight rough-hewn timber pillars, the broad pavilion was just big enough to squeeze everyone in. The adjoining shack served as their makeshift "kitchen," which made this shelter their communal dining hall.

Wei Wuxian arched a brow, strolling over with Wen Yuan still tucked under his arm. "What's the occasion? Nobody sleeping tonight? Where'd all these bright lanterns come from?"

Wen Qing stepped out of the adjacent kitchen carrying a steaming platter, shooting him a deadpan look. "Hung them up for you, your highness. We're making more tomorrow to line the mountain trail. You spend half your life stumbling around in the dark; it's only a matter of time before you slip off a cliff and break every bone in your body."

Wei Wuxian chuckled, "Even if I snap a bone or two, don't I have you to patch me up?"

"I don't work overtime for free," Wen Qing retorted sharply. "If you snap something, don't come crying to me when I reset your bones with a heavy hand."

Wei Wuxian shuddered theatrically and beat a hasty retreat into the pavilion. The moment he stepped inside, the crowd scrambled to shuffle aside, clearing a wide path for him. Three long tables had been set up, each groaning under the weight of seven or eight piping-hot dishes.

Wei Wuxian blinked. "What, nobody ate yet?"

Wen Qing set the platter down. "Nope. Everyone was waiting on you."

"Waiting on me for what? I already ate down in town."

The moment the words slipped past his teeth, he knew he'd screwed up.

Sure enough, Wen Qing slammed the platter onto the wooden table with a resounding clatter, sending the bright red chili peppers bouncing in the broth. Her eyes blazed with fury. "No wonder you came back empty-handed! You blew our entire budget stuffing your face at a tavern, didn't you?! I scraped together every last copper we had and handed it to you, and you go and blow it living like a king?!"

"No! Wait, I didn't—"

Right then, Granny Wen came hobbling out of the kitchen, leaning heavily on her wooden walking stick with one hand while precariously balancing a plate with the other. Wen Yuan wriggled out from under Wei Wuxian’s elbow, dropping to the dirt and sprinting over: "Granny!"

Wen Qing instantly abandoned her tirade, rushing over to relieve the old woman of the dish, grumbling under her breath, "Didn't I tell you to sit down and leave the cooking to us? The smoke in there is terrible for your chest! Your legs are bad and your hands shake—if you drop a plate, we don't have spares to replace it! Getting porcelain up this mountain takes an act of the gods..."

Around them, the rest of the Wen cultivators bustled about, neatly laying out chopsticks, pouring fresh water, and deliberately saving the seat of honor at the head of the table for him. Watching them fuss, Wei Wuxian suddenly felt an uncomfortable prickle of awkwardness.

In the past, he hadn't been blind to the fact that these people were genuinely terrified of him.

Every single soul here had heard of the blood-soaked legends trailing the Yiling Laozu during the Sunshot Campaign. They’d heard the whispered horror stories of his brutal, unhinged vengeance, and they had seen him command legions of the dead to tear living flesh apart with their own eyes. During those first few weeks, Granny Wen's knees would knock together whenever he so much as walked past, and little Wen Yuan had hidden behind her skirts for days before working up the nerve to inch closer.

Yet right now, more than fifty pairs of eyes were fixed on him. The lingering trace of fear was still there, but it was the quiet awe of reverence—laced with tentative, eager-to-please care. And beneath that, plain as day, was the exact same boundless gratitude and gentle warmth that shone in the eyes of the Wen siblings.

Wen Qing spoke in a soft, subdued murmur: "You've worked yourself to the bone these past few months. Thank you."

Wei Wuxian blinked, unsettled. "You... talking to me with actual manners? I'm genuinely terrified right now."

Wen Qing’s knuckles popped with a sharp, audible crack, and Wei Wuxian snapped his jaw shut on instinct.

Yet her voice remained quiet, uncharacteristically gentle.

"...They’ve wanted to sit down for a proper meal with you for a long time. Just to say thank you. But you’re always running around like a madman or locking yourself inside the Demon-Subduing Cave for days on end, refusing to let anyone near. They were terrified of getting in your way or getting on your nerves. They honestly thought you hated dealing with people and didn't want anything to do with them, so nobody dared bother you. But A-Ning woke up today. Fourth Uncle swore that no matter what, we were going to get you to sit at the table with us... So even if you stuffed yourself to bursting down in town, just sit down. You don't have to eat. Just sit with us, talk a little, and have a drink."

Wei Wuxian’s ears perked up, his eyes widening. "A drink? There's liquor on this rock?!"

Several elderly Wen men had been watching the exchange with held breath; hearing his interest, one of them beamed instantly, nodding eagerly. "Yes, yes! We have liquor, plenty of it!" He hastily grabbed a few sealed earthen jars from the corner, proudly presenting them like prized trophies. "Fruit wine! Brewed from wild mountain berries we gathered ourselves. It smells incredible!"

Wen Ning was crouched quietly beside the table, murmuring, "Fourth Uncle... loves his drink too. He knows how to brew it. Made it specially for tonight. Took him days of experimenting."

Because he forced himself to articulate every syllable slowly and deliberately, his old stutter had miraculously vanished. Fourth Uncle scratched the back of his neck with an embarrassed, slightly anxious chuckle, still eyeing Wei Wuxian with quiet nervousness.

Wei Wuxian grinned. "Is that so? Well, in that case, I have to try it!"

He pulled up a wooden bench and sat down. Fourth Uncle eagerly cracked the wax seal, presenting the opened jar with both hands. Wei Wuxian took a deep whiff, smiling broadly. "Damn, that really does smell amazing!"

With his lead, the rest of the family finally broke into relieved grins, pulling up benches and taking their seats. It felt as though his single compliment had lifted an immense weight off their chests; laughter and chatter erupted instantly as pairs of bamboo chopsticks dove into the steaming bowls.

For the very first time in his life, Wei Wuxian knocked back a drink without tasting a single note of it.

A stray thought drifted through his mind: Walking a single-log bridge until it goes pitch black... huh?

It's really not that dark at all.

A sudden, invigorating warmth washed through his limbs, untangling every knot of tension in his chest.

Fifty-odd people crammed together across three rickety wooden tables, chopsticks darting and clattering in a chaotic dance of domestic warmth. Wen Yuan was perched comfortably on his grandmother's lap, proudly showing off his new treasures, clacking his wooden sword and saber together in an epic miniature duel that had the toothless old woman giggling until her eyes vanished into crinkles.

Over on Wei Wuxian's end, he and Fourth Uncle had launched into an impassioned, animated debate over every regional vintage they’d ever tasted, ultimately concluding that Gusu’s famed Emperor’s Smile was the undisputed, peerless king of spirits.

Wen Qing circled the tables, pouring generous splashes of the homemade berry wine for the elders and retainers. Two rounds in, the clay jar came up bone-dry.

Wei Wuxian stared into his empty cup, aghast. "How is it gone already?! I barely had three sips!"

Wen Qing snatched the jar away. "There are only a few jars left, and we're rationing them. You're cut off for the night."

"You can't be serious!" Wei Wuxian protested. "As the ancient poets said: 'Better to enjoy a cup of wine right now than leave behind an empty, hollow name after death!' Enough nagging, pour me another, thank you very much!"

Given the occasion, Wen Qing relented, topping off his cup with a warning glare. "This is the only exception. You drink entirely too much; you need to swear off the bottle."

Wei Wuxian scoffed, "We're not at the Cloud Recesses! Swear off drinking? Over my dead body!"

At the mention of the Cloud Recesses, Wen Qing paused, giving him a pointed, calculated look before tossing out with deliberate nonchalance, "I forgot to ask—you’ve never brought an outsider up to the Burial Mounds before. What was that about today?"

Wei Wuxian shrugged. "You mean Lan Zhan? Just bumped into him in town."

"Bumped into him? Just like that? Another chance encounter?"

"Yeah."

Wen Qing arched a skeptical brow. "What a coincidence. If memory serves, you two had a 'chance encounter' back in Yunmeng, too."

"Nothing strange about that," Wei Wuxian dismissed breezily. "Cultivators from other clans pass through Yunmeng and Yiling all the time."

"I heard you calling him straight by his birth name earlier. You've got some nerve."

Wei Wuxian waved a hand. "He calls me straight by mine too! It's nothing, we've been doing it since we were teenagers. Neither of us cares."

"Is that so?" Wen Qing murmured. "From what I hear, you two despise each other. Word on the street is that you're like fire and water—drawing steel the second you cross paths."

"You're listening to tabloid gossip," Wei Wuxian chuckled. "Sure, things were rocky back then, and during the Sunshot Campaign we had short fuses and traded blows a few times. But it was never as bad as the rumors made it out to be. We're fine."

Wen Qing held her tongue, letting the topic drop.

Before long, the platters were scraped clean to the glaze. Someone tapped the rim of their bowl with a chopstick, shouting, "A-Ning! Whip up another batch of stir-fry, will you?"

"Make a big portion! Dump it in a basin!"

"Where are we gonna find a basin for food?! The only basins we have are for washing our faces!"

Wen Ning, who had no need for mortal food, had been standing sentinel by the edge of the shelter the entire time. Hearing the call, he blinked slowly, murmuring, "Oh. Okay."

Seeing his chance to shine, Wei Wuxian vaulted to his feet. "Hold your horses! Let me handle it! Step aside, I've got this!"

Wen Qing looked at him with profound suspicion. "You actually know how to cook?"

Wei Wuxian puffed out his chest, arrogance practically dripping from his jaw. "Obviously! I can dazzle in the grand hall and command the kitchen! Just sit tight and prepare to be amazed."

The crowd broke into enthusiastic applause, their expectations soaring.

A few minutes later, Wei Wuxian swaggered back into the pavilion, proudly slamming two steaming, ominous platters onto the table with an unhinged smirk.

Wen Qing took one look at the charred, bubbling, pitch-black abomination and said deadpan, "From this day forward, stay ten leagues away from my kitchen."

Wei Wuxian defended his masterpiece vehemently: "Just try a bite! You can't judge a dish purely on aesthetics! One mouthful and you'll see—this is authentic flavor right here!"

"Authentic my ass!" Wen Qing snapped. "Look at A-Yuan—he took one bite and he's bawling his eyes out! Total waste of good ingredients. Nobody touch your chopsticks! Don't you dare stroke his ego!"

Within three days, an earth-shattering piece of intelligence tore through the prominent cultivation sects:

The rogue who had defected from the Jiang Clan and holed up in Yiling had successfully engineered the highest-tier fierce corpse the world had ever seen. The monster was blindingly fast, absurdly strong, felt zero pain, killed with ruthless precision, and—most terrifying of all—retained complete, lucid human intellect! In the field, it was an unstoppable, walking slaughterhouse!

A collective panic seized the great clans: Peace is dead! Wei Wuxian is definitely going to mass-produce these abominations, establish his own dark sect, and conquer the realm! And worst of all, impressionable young cultivators are bound to be seduced by the raw shortcuts of the demonic path, flocking to his banner in droves! The orthodox cultivation world is doomed!

In reality, however, the single greatest utility Wei Wuxian found for his newly awakened, indestructible fierce corpse... was having a tireless pack mule to haul groceries up the mountain.

Back in the day, Wei Wuxian could barely haul a single wooden crate up the slopes on his own. Now, Wen Ning could single-handedly drag an entire overloaded freight cart up the crags, with a lazy, bench-lounging Wei Wuxian casually kicking his boots up on top of the cargo for the ride.

Naturally, not a single soul outside the mountain believed that. After Wen Ning made a few dazzling, unintentional appearances during local night-hunts, swarms of aspiring rogue cultivators actually began making pilgrimages to Yiling, desperate to swear fealty to the "Grandmaster" and become his sworn disciples. The desolate, corpse-ridden wasteland suddenly saw a bustling, chaotic influx of unsolicited foot traffic.

Because Wei Wuxian’s perimeter corpses were strictly forbidden from initiating lethal attacks—settling for tossing unwanted trespassers into the briars and snarling in their faces—no one ever got seriously hurt, which only made the crowds at the foot of the mountain grow more brazen.

The tipping point came when Wei Wuxian spotted a massive, fluttering war banner emblazoned with the words: SUPREME DEMONIC OVERLORD, THE YILING LAOZU.

He had sprayed a mouthful of berry wine straight across the dirt. Mortified beyond belief, he stormed down the mountain, shamelessly confiscated all the tribute offerings they had left for "His Venerable Eminence," and promptly carved out a secret mountain trail on the opposite side of the peak to bypass the madness entirely.

One afternoon, while running errands in town with his tireless pack mule in tow, a familiar silhouette flickered past the mouth of a nearby alley.

Wei Wuxian’s gaze sharpened. Without making a sound, he slipped into the shadows, trailing the figure down the winding lane until they ducked into a secluded, quiet courtyard.

The moment he crossed the threshold, the heavy wooden gate slammed shut behind him.

A frigid, familiar voice cut through the silence: "Get out."

Jiang Cheng was standing behind the door. He was the one who had bolted the gate, and the command had been barked squarely at Wen Ning.

Jiang Cheng held grudges like iron, his burning hatred for the Wen Clan running bone-deep. On top of that, he had been unconscious during the entire time the Wen siblings had saved his life, leaving him entirely incapable of sharing Wei Wuxian's sense of moral indebtedness; his hostility toward Wen Ning was venomous, and he hadn't hesitated to draw blood during their staged duel.

Recognizing the Jiang Sect Leader, Wen Ning bowed his head submissively and slipped back outside without a word.

Standing in the center of the courtyard was a woman, a veiled bamboo hat obscuring her face, a heavy black traveling cloak draped over her shoulders.

A lump rose in Wei Wuxian’s throat. "...Shijie."

Hearing his voice, the maiden turned. She lifted the bamboo hat and unclasped the dark cloak, letting the heavy wool slide to the flagstones.

Beneath the travel grime lay a breathtaking, brilliant crimson bridal gown.

Jiang Yanli stood resplendent in her formal wedding silks, delicate cosmetics highlighting her gentle features with a radiant, blooming elegance.

Wei Wuxian took two halting steps forward, his voice cracking: "Shijie... what is this?"

Jiang Cheng scoffed dryly from the gate, "What does it look like? You think she's marrying you?"

Wei Wuxian snapped, "Shut your mouth."

Jiang Yanli spread her silken sleeves, a soft, timid blush coloring her cheeks. "A-Xian... I'm... getting married soon. I came so you could see me..."

A searing, prickling heat flooded Wei Wuxian's eyes.

He couldn't attend the ceremony. He would never be permitted to stand among the guests to watch his beloved sister exchange vows in her bridal splendor. So, defying every political risk, Jiang Cheng and Jiang Yanli had slipped away in secret, traveling all the way to Yiling just to lead him into this hidden courtyard—so that he, and he alone, could see his Shijie dressed as a bride.

It took several heavy seconds before Wei Wuxian managed a strained, trembling smile. "I know! I heard..."

Jiang Cheng raised a brow. "Who told you?"

"None of your business."

Jiang Yanli lowered her arms, a shy, slightly apologetic smile playing on her lips. "It's just me, though... You won't get to see the groom."

Wei Wuxian curled his lip in theatrical disgust. "Like hell I'd want to see that peacock."

He circled around her twice, taking in every embroidered golden thread, his eyes shining with unadulterated admiration. "You look incredible, Shijie!"

Jiang Cheng crossed his arms, muttering, "Told you, A-Jie. I said it looked amazing."

Jiang Yanli, always modestly self-aware, shook her head with gentle earnestness. "What the two of you say doesn't count. You're completely biased."

Jiang Cheng threw his hands up in defeat. "You don't believe me, and you don't believe him. Are you honestly waiting for a certain someone to say it before you finally believe it's pretty?"

Hearing that, Jiang Yanli’s blush deepened furiously, flushing crimson all the way to her delicate ears, outshining even the rouge on her cheeks. Desperate to change the subject, she blurted out, "A-Xian... help me choose a courtesy name."

Wei Wuxian blinked. "A courtesy name for who?"

Jiang Cheng grunted, "For my nephew who hasn't even been conceived yet."

The wedding hadn't even taken place, and they were already scheming courtesy names for their future nephew. Yet Wei Wuxian didn't find it the least bit odd. Without an ounce of hesitation, he tapped his chin, turning the syllables over in his head.

"Alright," he decided. "The next generation of the Lanling Jin Clan follows the Ru character generation. Let's name him Jin Rulan."

Jiang Yanli beamed. "That sounds lovely!"

Jiang Cheng scowled immediately. "Terrible. It sounds like Jin Ru Lan—as in the Lan Clan of Gusu. An heir of Lanling Jin and Yunmeng Jiang—why on earth should he aspire to be 'like the Lans'?"

Wei Wuxian argued, "What's wrong with the Lan Clan? The orchid is a gentleman among flowers, and the Lans are gentlemen among men. It's a great name!"

"That's certainly not how you used to talk about them," Jiang Cheng sneered.

"She asked me to name him, not you! What are you nitpicking for?"

Jiang Yanli hurriedly intervened, "Alright, alright, you know how A-Cheng gets. It was actually his idea to ask you for the name in the first place. Stop bickering, both of you. I brought soup—wait here."

She slipped into the side room to fetch the crock. Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng traded a brief, silent glance. A moment later, Jiang Yanli returned, handing each of them a steaming porcelain bowl. Then, picking up a third, smaller bowl, she walked to the courtyard gate, smiling softly at the figure standing guard outside.

"Pardon the small dish, Wen Ning. This one is for you."

Wen Ning had been standing with his chin tucked to his chest, rigid as a stone pillar. Caught completely off guard, his resurrected cognitive faculties short-circuited into an immediate, flustered stammer: "A-Ah... t-there's a bowl for me too?"

Jiang Cheng grumbled from the courtyard, "Why does he get one?!"

Jiang Yanli scolded him gently, "I brewed an entire pot; everyone gets a share."

Wen Ning cradled the piping-hot bowl with trembling hands, mumbling in flustered gratitude: "Thank you, Lady Jiang... thank you so much."

He stared down at the rich broth, entirely at a loss. He was desperately embarrassed to admit the truth: he couldn't eat it. Giving it to him was a total waste. Dead men didn't have functioning digestive tracts.

Noticing his awkward hesitation, Jiang Yanli gently inquired after his condition, quietly striking up a warm, easy conversation with him at the threshold.

Inside the courtyard, Wei Wuxian and Jiang Cheng stood shoulder to shoulder. Jiang Cheng lifted his bowl in a mocking salute. "A toast to the formidable Yiling Laozu."

Hearing that dreaded title, the mental image of that gaudy, fluttering war banner with its shimmering golden embroidery flashed across Wei Wuxian’s mind. He hissed through his teeth, "Shut up!"

Taking a sip of the warm broth, Jiang Cheng asked quietly, "How's the stab wound from last time?"

"Healed ages ago."

"Mm." Jiang Cheng paused, swirling his soup. "How many days did it take?"

"Less than a week," Wei Wuxian said. "Told you, with Wen Qing around, it's child's play. Though you really didn't pull your punch, you bastard. You ran me clean through."

Jiang Cheng chewed on a tender piece of lotus root. "You're the one who had your corpse shatter my arm first. You took seven days; I had my arm in a sling for over a month."

Wei Wuxian smirked, entirely unrepentant. "Had to make it look convincing, didn't we? Besides, it was your left arm—doesn't stop you from doing paperwork. They say broken bones take a hundred days to mend; keeping it in a sling for three months wouldn't have killed you."

From the alleyway came the faint, halting murmurs of Wen Ning chatting with Jiang Yanli.

After a heavy silence, Jiang Cheng looked over. "Is this really how you're going to live from now on? Do you have any actual plans?"

"Not at the moment," Wei Wuxian murmured. "The people on the mountain are terrified of setting foot outside, and when I head down to town, nobody dares cross me. As long as I don't go out of my way to stir up trouble, we'll be fine."

"'Don't go out of your way'?" Jiang Cheng scoffed bitterly. "Wei Wuxian, do you honestly believe that if you don't look for trouble, trouble won't come looking for you? Saving a single life takes miracles, but ruining a man? There are ten thousand different ways to orchestrate a downfall."

Wei Wuxian stared into his bowl, his voice dropping low and unyielding: "Absolute power crushes every trick in the book. Let them bring their ten thousand plots—whoever steps up, I'll put them in the ground."

Jiang Cheng’s tone flattened into icy detachment. "You've never listened to a single word of advice I've ever given you. But mark my words: one day, you will realize that I was right all along."

He drained the last drop of soup in one swallow, setting the bowl down firmly. "Formidable. Truly peerless. As expected of the grand Yiling Laozu."

Wei Wuxian spat a bone into his palm, scowling. "Are you done yet?"

As they prepared to part ways, Jiang Cheng warned, "Don't bother walking us out. If someone spots us, it's over."

Wei Wuxian nodded. He knew full well the monumental risk the siblings had taken to sneak out here today. If an outsider caught wind of this reunion, the grand performance they had staged with their own blood would crumble into dust.

"We'll head out first," Wei Wuxian said softly.

Stepping into the alley, Wei Wuxian took point, with Wen Ning silently trailing a pace behind him. Suddenly, Wei Wuxian glanced over his shoulder, deadpan. "Why the hell are you still holding that bowl of soup?"

"Huh?" Wen Ning clutched the porcelain defensively to his chest, looking entirely reluctant to part with it. "Taking it back... I can't drink it, but... but someone else on the mountain can..."

Wei Wuxian stared at him for a long beat, then sighed, shaking his head. "Whatever. Hold it steady and don't spill a drop."

He turned back toward the mountain trail.

Deep down, he knew that it would be an agonizingly long time before he ever laid eyes on the family he had left behind.

Yet... wasn't he heading back to see his family right now?
